report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. text.text: According to the Visual attention span (VAS) hypothesis, the ability to identify a briefly presented sequence of visual elements (usually consonants) aids reading acquisition independently of skills related to the sounds of a language (phonology).
A new test with a reduced memory load addressed concerns about a phonological memory confound in traditional VAS tests.
In this PreProbe test, a probe letter was presented before each trial and the task was to decide whether it occurred in the brief five-letter sequence.
A correlational study with 264 adults assessed the relationships of VAS, phonological skills, and print exposure with both word-reading and spelling.
Both PreProbe and the traditional partial report VAS (PosProbe) had modest correlations with the literacy measures, and also with the measures of phonological skills.
In regression analyses, two phonological measures explained over 30% of literacy variance independently of VAS, while each VAS measure uniquely explained a maximum of 3%.
VAS may reflect achievement in phonological and literacy skills, and has at best a minor causal role in literacy.

Intensive psychological research since the 1980s has established that skills regarding the sounds of language (phonology) are vital in literacy acquisition in alphabetic languages such as English (e. g., 2018).
Training in phonological sensitivity, the ability to discriminate and manipulate sound units in aurally presented words facilitates reading acquisition (Bradley & Bryant, 1985).
text.formatted: Training in phonological sensitivity, the ability to discriminate and manipulate sound units in aurally presented words facilitates reading acquisition <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Bradley & Bryant, 1985)</ref>.

text.text: A typical phonological sensitivity task for older children and adults is Spoonerisms (change snail-track to trail-snack), with oral responses.
Phonological sensitivity likely supports reading acquisition indirectly by providing a foundation for phonological coding.
The latter skill involves mapping between spelling (orthography) and phonological units such as phonemes.
Phonological coding skill is typically assessed by having respondents pronounce word-like nonwords (pseudowords) from print (here, PWPron).
There is abundant evidence for a strong association between phonological sensitivity and coding in children and adults (Burt, 2006; Shapiro et al., 2013).
text.formatted: There is abundant evidence for a strong association between phonological sensitivity and coding in children and adults <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Burt, 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Shapiro et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: As Share (1995) proposed, phonological coding supports reading acquisition by unlocking the connection between words used in speech and their orthography.
text.formatted: As <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Share (1995)</ref> proposed, phonological coding supports reading acquisition by unlocking the connection between words used in speech and their orthography.

text.text: Researchers generally agree that phonological skill deficits cause most cases of dyslexia (Melby-Lervåg et al., 2012).
text.formatted: Researchers generally agree that phonological skill deficits cause most cases of dyslexia <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Melby-Lervåg et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Alternative theories propose that some cases of dyslexia are caused by deficits independent of phonological skills.
Here we assess one such theory, the Visual Attention Span (VAS) hypothesis (Bosse et al., 2007).
text.formatted: Here we assess one such theory, the Visual Attention Span (VAS) hypothesis <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Bosse et al., 2007)</ref>.

text.text: The hypothesis that VAS is a causal factor in reading acquisition was proposed by Bosse and Valdois (2003).
text.formatted: The hypothesis that VAS is a causal factor in reading acquisition was proposed by <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Bosse and Valdois (2003)</ref>.

text.text: VAS was defined as the number of visually presented elements (e.g., letters, shapes, coloured dots) a person could process in a single glance in a multielement visual display.
Bosse and Valdois proposed that their task tapped the size of the visual attentional window, with a large window reflecting skill in visual attention.
They stressed that this skill is independent of phonology in its contribution to reading development.
The computational model on which VAS is based (Ans et al., 1998) is concerned with the identification of fixated letters as the first stage of word reading.
text.formatted: The computational model on which VAS is based <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Ans et al., 1998)</ref> is concerned with the identification of fixated letters as the first stage of word reading.

text.text: There is no suggestion that readers attempt to remember letters; however, memory is required for verbal report of letters or digits in typical VAS tests.
The present view is that the size of a visual attentional window is not due to a cognitive skill that varies in a consistent way over individuals and across materials.
Experience at identifying the visual stimuli of VAS tasks can be expected to have a large effect on the number of items that can be processed under time pressure.
Furthermore, as discussed later, remembering and reporting letters or digits requires phonological coding.
The involvement of phonological coding in VAS tasks with nameable items may be partly responsible for its correlation with reading.
Following Bosse et al. (2007), VAS tests typically involve strings of 5 upper case consonants, presented for 200 ms.
text.formatted: Following <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Bosse et al. (2007)</ref>, VAS tests typically involve strings of 5 upper case consonants, presented for 200 ms.

text.text: Digits have sometimes been used.
The typical, whole report, VAS test, has participants report all letters in any order immediately after the display.

In a partial report version, which has similar associations with literacy, a bar is presented next to one of five letter-position markers shown immediately after the letters, and participants must indicate which letter had occupied that position.
Good performance in partial report requires that participants remember all letters and their positions.

There is a large literature documenting the relationship between VAS and reading ability, primarily through correlations and reader group comparisons, but no compelling evidence for a causal role of VAS in reading acquisition.
In the following section we briefly review these studies.

Associations between VAS and reading ability (word naming) have been reported in comparisons of dyslexic children and controls (Bosse et al., 2007; Bosse & Valdois, 2003), in large correlational studies of typical children (Bosse & Valdois, 2009; Lobier et al., 2012) and in meta-analyses (e. g., Gavril et al., 2021).

text.text: In summary, VAS generally has been found to be associated with word reading ability and, where examined, spelling.
Increased reading skill (and experience) entails increased letter identification skill, which, in turn, presumably affects VAS performance with letters and digits.
This issue of reverse causation in the VAS-reading relationship is explicitly addressed by reading-level designs.
Samples of dyslexic children are compared on VAS with younger children of the same reading age.
Superior performance of the reading-age-matched controls on VAS is taken to rule out the possibility that VAS performance is driven by reading skill.
There is some evidence for poorer VAS in dyslexia in reading-level design (Bosse & Valdois, 2003; Zoubrinetzky et al., 2014).

text.text: A concern about these studies is that Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD), was not controlled.
It is estimated that 20-40% of people diagnosable with dyslexia are diagnosable with ADHD (Germanò et al., 2010).

text.text: In summary, the evidence addressing reverse causation is inconsistent, with lack of ADHD screening possibly an issue in studies confirming a VAS disadvantage in dyslexia relative to reading level controls.
Ideally, the causal role of VAS in reading acquisition would be tested in pre-readers in training experiments or longitudinal studies, to rule out alternative explanations.
Such approaches are not useful in adults who are already proficient readers, as in the current study.

To date, the studies in children of various ages have not provided causal evidence for a causal role of VAS in reading, with two training studies having no untrained control (Valdois et al., 2014; Zoubrinetzky et al., 2019).

text.text: Typically, relative to an untrained control, attentional training with children produces an improvement in VAS but no significant improvement in reading (Ren et al., 2023; Valdois et al., 2025).

text.text: With respect to longitudinal evidence, van den Boer and de Jong (2018) found no evidence of a causal role in reading ability in VAS in grade 3-4 children.

A second longitudinal study (Valdois et al., 2019) found that VAS in kindergarten predicted reading in Grade 1, but there was no assessment of reverse causation, namely, an effect of literacy skills at T1 on VAS at T2.

text.text: In summary, the lack of evidence from well-controlled training and longitudinal studies for a causal role of VAS in reading acquisition suggests that further examination of the VAS task is warranted.
As noted above, a shared reliance on phonological coding skills may be responsible for the correlation between VAS tests and reading.
It is important to establish whether VAS predicts literacy skills when minimal phonological coding is required for successful report of items.
This issue is the focus of the present study.

Although VAS typically does not correlate with phonological sensitivity when age is controlled (Zoubrinetzky et al., 2016), VAS usually correlates with PWPron, the measure of phonological coding (Bosse et al., 2007; Bosse & Valdois, 2009; Valdois et al., 2021).

text.text: These findings work against the VAS hypothesis: A visual attentional deficit in dyslexia should be observed with all visual stimuli.

However, a problem is that the mean and standard deviation of accuracy with the less-nameable symbols are generally low, especially in adult studies, and floor compression may have prevented group differences from appearing.
We retained letter stimuli but addressed the phonological skills confound by comparing a conventional VAS test with a VAS test modified to have a minimal memory requirement (hereafter PreProbe).

The aim was to assess the role of memory demands (and thus phonological coding skills) in associations of typical VAS tests with reading, while avoiding the problem of low accuracy found with unnameable VAS items.
In PreProbe, our adult participants saw a probe letter just before a brief 5-letter sequence, after which they judged whether the sequence had contained the probe.

This lettersearch test, like traditional VAS tests, requires rapid identification of letters, with identification of all letters required when the probe is absent or the matching letter is in the last position.
As in traditional VAS tests, the larger the "attentional window", the better the ability to process the whole letter sequence in a brief display.
In contrast to traditional VAS tests, there is no requirement to remember all briefly displayed sequence letters or their position.
A minimal memory load is imposed by the requirement to hold a single, clearly displayed, probe letter for several hundred ms.
We compared the prediction of literacy by the PreProbe test versus the standard partial report test having a position probe after the sequence (hereafter, PosProbe).
We added spelling production to word reading as a literacy measure, thus allowing a novel comparison between the literacy tasks in their associations with VAS.

Finally, we evaluated VAS against traditional predictors of literacy, namely, phonological sensitivity, phonological coding, and print exposure, assessed respectively by a Spoonerism task, PWPron, and the Author Recognition Test (ART).

Several adult studies have assessed the relationship between VAS and reading (Collis et al., 2013; Li et al., 2021; Yeari et al., 2017), but none has assessed associations of VAS with phonological skills or print exposure.

text.text: Given the importance of acquiring orthographic representations for reading, we expected that any predictor of reading should also predict spelling.

If VAS facilitates reading acquisition, then accuracy in both VAS tests should predict reading and spelling, just as phonological skills, acknowledged facilitators of reading development, predict reading in adults (Pennington et al., 1987).

text.text: If instead the association of standard VAS tests with literacy reflects a memory confound, then PosProbe VAS performance should predict literacy, whereas the low-memory PreProbe test should not.
Furthermore, if PWPron (phonological coding) correlates with standard VAS tests because of a memory confound, it should correlate only with the PosProbe (partial report) test.

text.text: Because the PreProbe test was designed to have a negligible memory load, it was expected to show little impact of participants' phonological skills.
Therefore, a major hypothesis was that PreProbe VAS would not correlate with PWPron (phonological coding), WordID, or spelling.
This hypothesis was disconfirmed; all three correlations were small but significant, ranging from .22 to .26.
Regarding the traditional VAS measure, PosProbe, moderate correlations with PWPron, WordID and spelling were expected, in line with the developmental literature.
In fact, PosProbe correlated modestly at .22 to .30 with these predictors.
The VAS measures were expected to correlate weakly or non-significantly with phonological sensitivity as measured by the Spoonerism task.

However, both VAS measures had positive associations with Spoonerism accuracy similar to those observed for PWPron, perhaps reflecting the high difficulty and large variance of the present Spoonerism task.

A second question was whether VAS scores showed a relationship with the ART (print exposure), indicating that VAS may depend upon literacy skill and experience rather than being a causal factor in literacy acquisition.
This hypothesis had some support, with a small correlation (r = .13, p = .035) observed between PreProbe and the ART.
Unlike PreProbe, the PosProbe test did not show a correlation with the ART.
However, this null result may reflect a counter-confounding effect of age, which had a negative correlation with PosProbe and a moderately high positive association with the ART.
When age was partialled out, PosProbe and the ART tended to show a correlation, r = .11, p = .069. et al. (2007) argued that VAS aids reading independently of phonological skills.

text.text: Therefore, the two phonological measures were entered together in hierarchical multiple regression analyses (HMR), and their importance relative to each VAS test was assessed separately for WordID and spelling.

text.text: The latter result may reflect the working memory demands of PosProbe and Spoonerisms.
Importantly, overall, the two VAS tests (unexpectedly) showed similar associations with the DVs and the traditional predictors of literacy skills.
The correlations of the VAS tests with literacy were considerably lower than is typical in developmental studies.
It is possible that VAS is a causal factor in reading acquisition, but in well-practised adult readers it may not substantially limit reading performance.

Against this argument, phonological sensitivity plays no direct role in accomplished reading, yet the present adult sample showed a substantial correlation between literacy and the Spoonerism test of phonological sensitivity.
It appears that cognitive skills that are important for literacy acquisition continue to be associated with adult literacy (Castles et al., 2018; Pennington et al., 1987; Perfetti, 2007).

text.text: Likewise, if VAS indexes a causal variable that supports word identification, then it can be expected to support word identification in adults.
Consequently there is good reason to suppose that the present results with adults have implications for literacy development.
Results involving the traditional predictors were largely as expected.
Our observed correlation of r = .55 between WordID and spelling is typical for adults (Cunningham & Stanovich, 1990; Stanovich et al., 1991).

text.text: The ART is somewhat insensitive, and the mean corrected for false alarms was low.
Nonetheless, the present ART correlated moderately-to-strongly with WordID and spelling.
The correlation of the ART with PWPron, though larger than expected, aligns with evidence that reading experience impacts spelling-sound knowledge (Vellutino, 1994).

text.text: Individuals with good phonological skills may also find reading easier and thus read more than others.
This possibility may also explain the unexpected correlation of Spoonerisms with the ART.

As Ans et al. (1998) noted in their computational model that was the impetus for the VAS test, a global strategy for processing letter strings is employed for reading familiar words, whereas unfamiliar words and nonwords are largely read by an analytic strategy that segments letter strings. Van den Boer et al. (2015) observed that the association between phonological coding (PWPron) and VAS that is commonly reported cannot be based on the role of VAS as a measure of the global strategy, given that this strategy is not available for unfamiliar items.

text.text: The effectiveness of the global strategy (and hence VAS) is potentially relevant only to reading already-learned words, and thus is difficult to disentangle from reading experience.
Spelling is more heavily dependent on the quality of orthographic representations than is reading, with some effective readers being poor spellers (Andrews et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Spelling is more heavily dependent on the quality of orthographic representations than is reading, with some effective readers being poor spellers <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Andrews et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Establishing new orthographic representations for unfamiliar words must rely on the analytic strategy, and it is uncertain to what extent the global strategy supports the updating of orthographic representations.
Arguably, support for the VAS hypothesis would be stronger if VAS accuracy were more closely correlated with word reading than with pseudoword pronunciation or spelling.
Our evidence suggests that VAS-literacy associations are not independent of phonological skills.

Our VAS tests had similar associations with PWPron (coding) and Spoonerisms (sensitivity), perhaps reflecting the high demands of Spoonerisms, as well as the presumed causal role of sensitivity in the acquisition of coding skills.
As noted, phonological sensitivity often has non-significant correlations with VAS.
Phonological coding supports short term serial recall of verbal material (Baddeley & Hitch, 1994), and dyslexia is associated with deficits in this task (Rapala & Brady, 1990).
text.formatted: Phonological coding supports short term serial recall of verbal material <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Baddeley & Hitch, 1994)</ref>, and dyslexia is associated with deficits in this task <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Rapala & Brady, 1990)</ref>.

text.text: Consequently we expected that phonological coding would no longer predict VAS accuracy when the working memory demand was substantially reduced.
This expectation was disconfirmed; the PreProbe VAS test designed to have a low memory load, like the PosProbe test, showed small but significant correlations with literacy.
As indicated in the Results section, there are several sources of evidence that the memory load was successfully reduced for the PreProbe test.
We conclude that the VAS-literacy association may indeed depend on phonological coding but not necessarily on verbal working memory.

We discuss two possibilities below; namely, a direct effect of phonological coding on speeded letter identification, and an effect that arises in the context of a reverse causation account of the VAS-literacy association.
These possibilities cannot be evaluated as causes in the present cross-sectional correlational data, but potentially inform future research on VAS and its importance.
In addition to its role in literacy, phonological coding may support letter identification and decision making in VAS tasks.
The correlations between phonological sensitivity and VAS equally fit with this account given that phonological sensitivity is thought to play a causal role in phonological coding skill.

Pre-reading children at risk of dyslexia show weaker phonological skills and slower acquisition of letter knowledge (Hindson et al., 2005), while adults with weaker phonological skills may be slow to name letters.
text.formatted: Pre-reading children at risk of dyslexia show weaker phonological skills and slower acquisition of letter knowledge <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Hindson et al., 2005)</ref>, while adults with weaker phonological skills may be slow to name letters.

text.text: Proficient performance under time pressure in VAS tests plausibly relies not only on fluent letter identification, but also on the efficient use of letter names (phonology) in decision-making and response preparation.

As noted, in VAS tests with unnameable symbols instead of letters, mean accuracy has been low (less than 40%), except in a less demanding test in which children chose, after each trial, between the target and an item that did not appear in the sequence (Ziegler et al., 2010).

text.text: Low accuracy with symbols suggests an important role for item naming in VAS performance.

In our study, weaker phonological coding in some participants may have slowed letter name activation and, especially under time pressure, made their phonological representations noisier and more vulnerable to mutual interference.
In summary, phonological skills may support speeded letter identification in VAS and literacy, explaining the association between the latter two constructs.
We sought to test this explanation in an exploratory analysis.

A signature effect of the deployment of phonological coding in short-term serial recall tasks is the phonological similarity effect, namely, poorer ordered short-term recall when all list items are phonologically similar than when they are dissimilar (Baddeley & Hitch, 1994).

The VAS hypothesis would be most favoured if phonological similarity was unrelated to performance.

However, in both VAS tasks, trials on which the probe/target letter was phonologically similar to one other sequence letter (SIM) had higher accuracy and faster latencies (for correct responses) than trials with no similar sequence letter (DISS).

text.text: In summary, the results indicate that phonological similarity between a target and another sequence item facilitates letter naming and thus task accuracy in both VAS tasks.
In turn, this result weakens the view that VAS is a predictor or cause of literacy skills that is independent of phonological skills.

Another possible explanation for the associations between VAS and phonological skills is that reverse causation is at work: Reading skill and experience affect letter identification efficiency and VAS.
If this account is correct, the fact that phonological skills have a causal role in reading acquisition means that they in turn are likely to be associated with VAS.

There was only modest support for reverse causation in our results, with a small correlation (r = .13) between PreProbe and the ART measure of reading experience, and a trend (p = .069) for a correlation between PosProbe and the ART when age was controlled.
The correlation with the ART may be small because most university students and other highly literate adults have had sufficient reading practice to have reached a plateau on visual letter processing.
Therefore, many below-average scorers on the ART may have had sufficient reading experience to perform well on the VAS tests.
Consequently, the reverse causation hypothesis remains viable although the ART did not produce compelling evidence for it.

In line with a large body of evidence (Melby-Lervåg et al., 2012), the traditional predictors of literacy skills, namely phonological skills and reading experience, had moderate or strong relationships with literacy measures.

text.text: Meanwhile, the smaller VAS-literacy correlations in our adult sample, and in developmental studies controlling for age (and thus in part for reading experience and memory skills), work against the causal importance of VAS in reading development (Bosse et al., 2007; Saksida et al., 2016; Zoubrinetzky et al., 2016).

text.text: Additionally, after controlling phonological ability, the present VAS measures only weakly predicted literacy, with the PosProbe-spelling association becoming non-significant.
Thus, there was little support for VAS as an independent causal factor in reading acquisition.

The present cross-sectional correlational study cannot allow causal inferences to be drawn, but does suggest possible explanations for the small associations we observed between VAS and literacy measures.
Specifically, these associations might be explained as a) effects of phonological skills on speeded letter identification in VAS and on literacy or b) results of reading experience and skill.

In any case, the present results show, in line with the conclusions of Saksida et al. (Saksida et al., 2016), that any causal role of visual attention span in literacy acquisition is substantially less important than the role of phonological skills.

text.text: The aim of the present study with adults was to assess a new low-memory version of the VAS test (of letters) against a traditional partial report VAS test in its associations with literacy.

The study was novel in that both word reading and spelling were dependent measures, and a measure of print exposure was included to provide information on possible effects of reading experience on VAS.
Also novel in adult studies, the traditional predictors phonological skills and print exposure provided a benchmark against which to assess the prediction by VAS.
As expected, the two DVs WordID and spelling were strongly correlated.
The results for the VAS tests did not fully align with predictions or with prior findings by Valdois and colleagues (Bosse et al., 2007).

text.text: Both the partial report PosProbe test and the low-memory PreProbe test correlated weakly-to-moderately (r = .23 to .30) with WordID and spelling.

There was evidence that VAS is not independent of phonological abilities, given that the VAS tests also correlated weakly-to-moderately (r = .22 to .28) with both phonological coding (PWPron) and sensitivity (Spoonerisms).
Furthermore, phonological skills accounted for substantial variance in literacy unaccounted for by VAS, as expected, while VAS accounted for little unique variance.
Little change in the unique contribution of VAS was observed when PWPron was dropped from the phonological measures.
The pattern of associations suggests some conclusions about the nature of the connection between VAS tests and literacy.
Of course, no conclusions about causation can be drawn in the present cross-sectional correlational study.
The regression analyses indicate that the traditional PosProbe test had a slightly stronger unique association with word identification than PreProbe, but both associations were significant.
By contrast, for spelling, PreProbe made a small but significant unique prediction whereas PosProbe did not.
